readerTitle: The shop that was a little better and a little cheaper, and lost
caseNote: 가상 사례 (생활용품 가게, 사내 데이터 분석팀) + 실제 이론 (Porter, 1980/1985)
insight: 중간 위치가 위험한 이유는 가격이 어중간해서가 아니라, 어떤 고객에게도 우리를 고를 분명한 이유가 없어서다.
misconception: 조금 더 싸고 조금 더 좋으면 양쪽 고객을 모두 잡을 수 있다.

sources.text: Porter, M. E. (1980). Competitive Strategy. Free Press. ('stuck in the middle' 개념)
Porter, M. E. (1985). Competitive Advantage. Free Press.
가게와 사내 분석팀 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 'stuck in the middle'이라는 표현이 Porter(1980) Competitive Strategy에 처음 등장하는지, 1985년 저서에서 다시 다루는지 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 1980년 책으로만 적었습니다.
7번 카드의 '일부 기업은 원가와 차별화를 동시에 달성한다'는 비판은 후속 연구에서 널리 제기된 일반론으로만 적었습니다. 특정 기업이나 연구 수치는 넣지 않았습니다.
가게, 할인점, 부티크, 분석팀 상황은 모두 가상입니다. 수치는 사용하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The shop that was a little better and a little cheaper, and lost
body: Mara runs a homewares shop on a busy street. Her prices sit below the design boutique two doors down. Her shelves look nicer than the big discount store at the edge of town.
For years, that worked. Now both neighbors are growing, and her sales are slipping every month. Nothing about her shop has changed.

image.label: A mid-sized shop squeezed between a discount store and a boutique
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 거리 풍경. 왼쪽에 큰 할인 매장(가격표가 크게 보임), 오른쪽에 세련된 부티크(조명과 진열이 고급스러움), 가운데 평범한 생활용품 가게가 양쪽 건물 사이에 살짝 눌려 있는 모습. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You're Mara. What do you do?
body: Price-focused shoppers now drive to the discounter. Style-focused shoppers go to the boutique. You still have rent, staff and loyal regulars, but fewer each month.

options.text: Cut prices on best-sellers to match the discounter
options.feedback: You win back some bargain hunters, but the discounter buys in far bigger volumes. You'd match its prices without its costs, and lose money on your most popular items.

options.text: Keep prices steady and invest in friendlier, better service
options.feedback: Service can be a real reason to choose you. But it only works if it's clearly better than the boutique's, and if customers will pay for it.

options.text: Pick one group of customers and rebuild the shop around serving them best
options.feedback: You give up some shoppers on purpose. In return, one group gets a reason to choose you that neither neighbor offers.

cards.title: Each neighbor took the customers it served best.
body: The discounter is cheaper than Mara on almost everything. The boutique is more beautiful and more special. Each one is clearly the best at *something*.

Mara's shop is second-best at both. Her customers were never choosing her. They were choosing whatever was nearest. Once a clearly better option opened for each type of shopper, the reason to visit her shrank to convenience.

image.label: Shoppers splitting toward two stores, few in the middle
image.brief: 단순한 일러스트. 화면 가운데에서 쇼핑객들이 두 갈래로 갈라짐. 왼쪽 화살표 "Lowest price" 쪽 할인점, 오른쪽 화살표 "Most special" 쪽 부티크. 가운데 가게 앞에는 쇼핑객 한두 명만 남아 있음. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Stuck in the middle
body: **Stuck in the middle** describes a business that tries to be both cheaper and better, but ends up the cheapest at nothing and the best at nothing.

Michael Porter named the idea in his 1980 book *Competitive Strategy*. His point: customers pick the clear winner for what they care about. A business without a clear win for anyone gets squeezed from both sides.

cards.title: Low cost and being special pull in opposite directions.
body: The choices that make you cheapest often make you less special, and the reverse is also true.
list: **To be cheapest:** fewer products, bigger orders, plain stores, self-service
**To be special:** unusual products, expert staff, beautiful spaces, small batches
**In the middle:** some of each, so costs stay too high to win on price and the offer stays too ordinary to win on difference
cards.callout: Each half-step toward one side quietly undoes the other.

cards.title: The same squeeze shows up everywhere.
body: A restaurant with a 90-item menu can't match a fast-food chain on price or a chef's bistro on food. A mid-priced hotel can lose budget travelers to a cheaper brand and business travelers to a luxury one.
The warning sign is the same: when you ask why customers choose you, the honest answer is "we're not bad at anything."
cards.softwareNote: A tool that is pricier than free alternatives but has fewer features than the market leader is stuck in the middle. Users drift to the free option or upgrade to the leader. Narrowing to one type of user is often the way out.

cards.title: The middle isn't always fatal.
body: Being in the middle hurts most when strong rivals sit at both ends. In a small town with no discounter and no boutique, a middle shop can do fine.

Later researchers also pointed out that some companies do win on cost and quality at once, usually by running their operations better than anyone else. The real danger is drifting into the middle by accident, adding a bit of everything until no one can say what you stand for.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside a large company.
body: You lead the in-house data analysis team. Departments can build simple dashboards themselves with a self-service tool, or hire outside consultants for big, deep projects. Your team does a bit of both, and has a three-month backlog.
Departments are starting to go around you. What do you do?

options.text: Keep taking every request and work through the queue faster
options.feedback: Working harder keeps you in the middle. You'll still be slower than the self-service tool and less deep than the consultants.

options.text: Focus on high-stakes analysis only, and train departments to build routine dashboards themselves
options.feedback: You give up the easy requests on purpose. In return, you become the clear first choice for the work that matters most to the company.

options.text: Ask for more headcount so you can do both properly
options.feedback: More people clear the backlog for a while. But without a clear focus, you're still a costlier, slower version of both alternatives.

cards.title: Be the clear best for someone, or be the clear choice for no one.
body: Customers pick the winner for what they care about. Being decent at everything rarely wins.
**Try it today:** finish this sentence: "Customers choose us over everyone else because we are the most ___." If you can't fill the blank honestly, you may be in the middle.
